clue.text: Thank you: forty-day period for natural aptitude

parts.note: ta is the everyday British thank you, two letters said rather than written
Lent is the church's fast of forty days running from Ash Wednesday to Easter

explanation.surface: Gratitude for a forty-day stretch that brought out someone's natural gift.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon reads as a list of unrelated things and is really a join, which is most of the disguise here. Neither piece is hidden or turned, so the two simply run into each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A talent is the gift somebody is born with rather than one they trained for, which is exactly what makes an aptitude natural.

clue.text: Fool removed my bloomers at Bath venue!

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: removed as in moved about, so the letters of the underwear phrase are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A clown has taken off someone's bloomers at a venue in Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removed my bloomers' reads as undressing, but 'removed' means moved about. Bath is a Georgian spa city in England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Assembly Rooms in Bath are a celebrated eighteenth-century hall used for balls and social gatherings.

clue.text: Charm of another name belonging to us

indicators.note: another signals a different version, so the letters of name are put in another order

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder
our means belonging to us

explanation.surface: We own the charm of a different name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another name' reads as an alias, but 'another' asks for a different arrangement of the word's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour is to captivate or charm someone so they fall in love.

indicators.note: becomes signals that the letters turn into something else, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of twin is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Ted's twin brother has nearly turned bent and twisted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims the last letter of the twin, and 'becomes' then mixes what is left with Ted's.
explanation.definitionFit: Twisted and warped both mean bent out of shape, or perverted in mind.

clue.text: Stake put on swimmer to hand someone over to the enemy

definitions.text: hand someone over to the enemy

parts.note: money staked, put on a horse or a result, is a bet
a ray is the flat fish that glides along the seabed, a swimmer with no legs at all

explanation.surface: A wager on a swimmer, with a captive handed to the other side as the price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' wants to be a person in a race; in a grid it is almost always a fish. 'Stake put on' is one piece rather than two, because it takes the whole phrase to reach the gambling sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To betray a person is to give them up to the other side, the informer's act of delivering somebody into enemy hands.

parts.note: Borneo, the huge island shared between Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei
the O that love stands for, and the one the clue says is absent

explanation.surface: Somebody carried off to an island with no romance about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loveless' reads as a complaint about the island and is the instruction. Only one of the two Os can go and leave a word standing, so the final letter is the one meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Borne is the past participle of bear: a burden borne is a burden carried, as in 'borne aloft on their shoulders'.

indicators.note: In a down entry one thing on another sits above it, so the first piece is written at the top and the second underneath.

parts.note: a temp is the temporary staffer an agency sends in to cover a desk
t is the standard short form for time

explanation.surface: A treat dangled in front of the office temp at just the right hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is carrying the stacking order rather than joining two halves of a sentence, which is what makes it an instruction here and not mere glue. Office worker is the setter's nudge towards agency staff rather than towards any job title.
explanation.definitionFit: To tempt somebody is to dangle something in front of them until they want it, which is what luring does.

indicators.note: dilapidated means fallen into ruin, so the city's letters are broken and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder
a home is a dwelling

explanation.surface: A seat salvaged from a run-down house in Lancaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' looks like a chair, but it is the country seat of a family, and the city name is only the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A family's seat is its principal country house, inherited down the generations.

clue.text: See April turning out garden trellis

definitions.note: a frame on which fruit trees are trained flat; strictly the tree trained on it too

indicators.note: turning out here means the letters are turned over and come out in a new order

explanation.surface: An invitation to watch how April's weather turns out in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning out' rearranges the letters of SEE and APRIL together. 'turning out' reads as how things end up, not as a signal to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: An espalier is a lattice or framework against which fruit trees and shrubs are trained to grow flat.

parts.note: the letter the clue prints, taken exactly as it stands
the ace is the one — the single spot on a die, the one card in a suit

explanation.surface: The name of a nightspot somewhere off the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M is printed as it stands and the 1 wants its card-table name. The M1 is Britain's first motorway, London to Leeds, and that road is the whole of the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A mace is the medieval war club, a heavy shaft with a spiked head, so 'club' names it by its plain kind.

definitions.note: Ammo is a mass noun where 'bullets' is a plural, but the two stand in for each other freely in speech — out of ammo, out of bullets.

indicators.note: What holds something keeps it inside itself, so the word in front is carrying what is wanted within its own letters.

parts.note: four consecutive letters of the beast's name, starting one letter in

explanation.surface: A mammoth with a stash of bullets inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds' says to look inside rather than to build anything. The run starts one letter in and crosses no gap, which is the only way seven letters can carry four without a join showing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammo is the clipped form of ammunition, the rounds a gun is loaded with, which is what bullets are.

indicators.note: Say here means as you say it: the word beside it is being handed over by sound rather than by spelling.

parts.note: treaties are the formal agreements nations sign, and the plural is spoken just as the answer is

explanation.surface: A long essay on the sort of agreements diplomats sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' reads as 'for example' and is really asking for a sound. British speech ends the word with a z, which is what brings it level with the plural of treaty.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a long formal written study of one subject, which is what a dissertation is.

indicators.note: Something seen shortly is glimpsed only briefly, so the name in front stops before it reaches its last letter.

parts.note: Florida, the state on America's south-eastern corner, named by the Spanish for flowers

explanation.surface: A brief look at an American state full of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen shortly' is a glance on the surface and an instruction underneath: stop before the last letter. The definition and the state come from the same Spanish root, which is why the pair sit so close together.
explanation.definitionFit: Florid writing is flowery writing — ornate, overblown, more decoration than the sense needs — and a florid face carries the same excess in colour.

parts.note: re is the shorthand that heads a business letter, standing for regarding
the mark was Germany's money until the euro replaced it in 2002

explanation.surface: An observation about a coin from pre-euro Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is hidden or turned here, so the clue rests entirely on knowing the currency. Old is doing real work: the mark is out of circulation, which is what stops a modern coin being wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark is the thing you say in passing, which is what a comment is — he made a remark about the weather.

clue.text: Others mixing gin taking a break

parts.note: the rest are the others

indicators.note: mixing signals the letters of gin are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Other people are making gin cocktails while on a break.
explanation.definitionFit: Resting means pausing from work or activity to relax.

clue.text: Style of farm building suggests humbleness

parts.note: a mode is a manner or style — a mode of dress, a mode of travel
a sty is the pig's shed in a farmyard

explanation.surface: The look of a farm outbuilding gives off an air of humility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Style of farm building' reads as one architectural phrase and splits after the first word. The sty is the smallest and plainest thing on a farm, which is why the surface holds together so quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: Modesty is the habit of making little of yourself, which is humbleness of manner rather than humbleness of station.

clue.text: Hats for a pound one tries out

indicators.note: Letters put out are letters turned out of their places, and nothing turned out goes back in the order it left.

parts.note: lb is the shorthand for a pound in weight
the Roman numeral for one
five letters straight off the page, joining the other three

explanation.surface: Hats going for a pound each, and a shopper trying them on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is a letter here rather than the shopper the surface offers, and 'a pound' is the weight, not the price on the label. Eight letters go in and eight come out, so nothing is spare.
explanation.definitionFit: A trilby is the soft felt hat with a narrow brim and a crease along the crown, named after the heroine of du Maurier's novel.

clue.text: Taken in flat, tea — or coffee?

indicators.note: What is taken in is held inside, so the words that follow are carrying something within them.

parts.note: the five letters run on from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Asking whether the drink served in the flat was tea or coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma is where the run straddles, and punctuation never breaks a hidden answer — it is put there to make you stop. 'Flat' is the misdirection that costs most, because a flat white is a coffee too.
explanation.definitionFit: A latte is espresso let down with a lot of hot milk, so 'coffee' names it by the drink it is made from.

clue.text: Clumsy spinet lacks head and gets mixed up

indicators.note: gets mixed up means the remaining letters are jumbled into a new order
lacks head means the word's first letter is missing, so spinet loses its opening letter

parts.note: taken as written; a spinet is a small harpsichord

explanation.surface: A small harpsichord missing its top gets its parts jumbled, as a clumsy player might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacks head' drops the S from SPINET to leave PINET, and 'gets mixed up' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept describes someone lacking skill or awkward in doing things, a close synonym for clumsy.

parts.note: the clue's first word lifted straight off the page
le is the French for the, in its masculine form

explanation.surface: A question about whether the French share things out.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the sentence as a stretched reading rather than a plain question. In Britain the same word names unemployment benefit, from this very sense of handing things round in portions.
explanation.definitionFit: To dole something out is to give it away in measured shares, the sense kept in 'doled out the rations'.

parts.note: lo is the old word for look, kept alive in 'lo and behold'
st is the short form of saint, as written before a name

explanation.surface: A call to notice that a decent man came off worst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look' reads as an address to the listener and is the archaic exclamation. Saints supply those two letters so often that 'good person', 'holy man' and 'church father' all come to the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A side that lost suffered defeat, the past tense matching so the two swap straight over.

parts.note: e is the standard short form for English, as on a language label
a mission is the task somebody is sent out on, a quest by another name

explanation.surface: An English expedition sent out to trace where something is draining away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To find' is joinery and contributes nothing, so the two pieces run straight on. An emission is a discharge rather than a current, so 'outflow' is being used of gases and fumes as much as of liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: An emission is whatever is given off and sent out — exhaust from a car, light from a lamp — so it flows outward from its source.

parts.note: the article is a letter of the answer here rather than joinery
the scent is the trail a fox leaves for the hounds to follow

explanation.surface: A footpath running up a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is material rather than an article, which is the easiest thing to skip past in six letters. The surface paints the very thing the definition names, so there is almost no gap between the two readings.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is the rise you climb — 'a steep ascent out of the village' names the slope itself, which is the sense hill carries here.

clue.text: Listened to guy spring at intervals

indicators.note: What you listen to reaches you as sound, so the word beside it is to be taken by ear and not by its spelling.

parts.note: a geezer is a bloke in British slang, and the two words are said the same way

explanation.surface: Listening to a bloke leap up every now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' wants to be the verb the surface bloke is doing and is the noun of water. The British pronunciation is what makes the pair match — said the American way, with a long i, nothing rhymes.
explanation.definitionFit: A geyser is a hot spring that fires a column of water into the air every so often instead of flowing steadily.
